sec.title: Objective
sec.p: Pembrolizumab plus platinum and pemetrexed (Pemb-Plt-PEM) combination therapy is an effective first-line treatment for advanced non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), regardless of programmed death-ligand 1 expression. However, the effectiveness and feasibility of first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy in elderly patients (≥75 years old) remain unclear. Therefore, this study investigated the safety and efficacy of first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM in elderly patients with non-squamous NSCLC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We retrospectively evaluated the data of patients ≥75 years old with non-squamous NSCLC who were treated with first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM from December 2018 to December 2020 at 10 institutes in Japan. Data on patient characteristics, efficacy of Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy, and the type and severity of adverse events were reviewed.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Thirty patients [20 men and 10 women; median age: 76 (range: 75-82) years old] were included in the analysis. The overall response rate, disease control rate, median progression-free survival (PFS), and median overall survival (OS) were 40.0%, 66.7%, 7.5 and 24.0 months, respectively. The treatment-related deaths were caused by pneumonitis. First-line Pemb-Plt-PEM was associated with the PFS, based on the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR). The PFS for low and high NLR values was 10.1 and 2.0 months, respectively. Furthermore, the sex and NLR influenced the association between Pemb-Plt-PEM and the OS. The OS for low and high NLR values was 32.8 and 2.6 months, respectively.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: First-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy is effective and feasible in elderly patients with non-squamous NSCLC.
Keywords: advanced non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer, elderly patients, first-line chemotherapy, pemetrexed, pembrolizumab, PD-L1
Received 2024 Feb 17; Accepted 2024 Mar 31; Issue date 2025 Jan 1.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Lung cancer is the most common malignancy worldwide, causing approximately 25% of all cancer-related deaths in 2021 (1). The number of elderly individuals with advanced lung cancer is increasing worldwide owing to the aging of the population (2). The incidence of thoracic malignancies increases with age. Epidemiological studies have reported that ＞50% of patients with lung cancer are ≥65 years old, which is the lower limit for defining the “elderly” population in epidemiological studies (3). Although the incidence and prevalence of cancer are increasing among patients ≥75 years old, ＜10% of patients enrolled in the National Cancer Institute collaborative group studies have non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC); this subpopulation is therefore often underestimated in clinical studies (4,5).

The efficacy of carboplatin plus pemetrexed therapy followed by pemetrexed maintenance therapy was equivalent to that of docetaxel monotherapy in patients ≥75 years old with advanced non-squamous NSCLC (6). Furthermore, the efficacy and safety of pembrolizumab plus platinum and pemetrexed (Pemb-Plt-PEM) combination therapy for advanced non-squamous NSCLC were demonstrated in a phase 3 KEYNOTE-189 study (7-9). Over 10.5 months (median) of follow-up, Pemb-Plt-PEM improved the overall survival [overall survival (OS) hazard ratio (HR): 0.49; p＜0.001] and progression-free survival (PFS; HR: 0.52; p＜0.001), irrespective of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, compared to placebo plus platinum and pemetrexed (7). Treatment benefits were consistently reported after a median follow-up of 23.1 months (8) and 31.0 months (9), respectively.

In addition, Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy has a feasible safety profile. A meta-analysis reported that combination therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and cytotoxic drugs for NSCLC in elderly patients is as effective as that in young patients (10). However, the cutoff age for elderly patients with NSCLC was 65 years old, and the PFS was significantly shorter in elderly patients (≥65 years old) than in younger patients (＜65 years old) who received pembrolizumab and cytotoxic drug combination therapy for NSCLC. In the KEYNOTE-189 study, the hazard ratio of death was higher in patients ≥75 years old than in younger patients, according to the assessment report of the European Medicines Agency (11). Several studies have investigated the efficacy and safety of ICI and cytotoxic drug combination therapy in the elderly, but reports focusing on Pemb-Plt-PEM are scarce, and the number of patients ≥75 years old is even smaller and inconclusive (12,13). Thus, whether or not first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy in elderly patients (≥75 years old) is effective and feasible is unclear. It is also unclear which clinical factors influence treatment efficacy in the elderly. Furthermore, it would be useful to classify elderly patients into benefitting and non-benefitting populations for ICI and cytotoxic drug therapy based on blood tests.

This study retrospectively evaluated the efficacy and safety of first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy in elderly patients (≥75 years old) with advanced non-squamous NSCLC. Furthermore, this study examined the significance of the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), a prognostic marker for ICI treatment (14-16) that can be easily measured in clinical practice, in first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy in the elderly.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: We retrospectively analyzed the efficacy and safety of first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy administered to patients with non-squamous NSCLC at 10 Japanese institutions between December 2018 and December 2020. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the International Medical Center, Saitama Medical University (number 2022-036) approved the study protocol. The requirement for written informed consent was waived because this was a retrospective study. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) histologically or cytologically confirmed non-squamous NSCLC at inoperable disease stage III/IV or postoperative recurrent disease and (2) the use of Pemb-Plt-PEM as first-line treatment.

Initially, 248 patients who received Pemb-Plt-PEM as the first-line treatment were selected. Among them, 11 patients with positive druggable driver gene mutations/translocations received molecular-targeted therapy as first-line treatment. A significant amount of data was missing for one patient. Eventually, 30 of 236 elderly patients (≥75 years old) were included in our analysis (Fig. 1). The pathological diagnosis and staging of NSCLC followed the 2015 World Health Organization classification and tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) staging system version 8 (17). TNM stages were assigned based on the findings of a physical examination, plain chest radiography, thoracic and abdominal computed tomography, bone scintigraphy or 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging. A medical chart investigation was performed for each patient at each institution. We reviewed the medical records for baseline characteristics, treatment responses to first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy, whether or not second-line chemotherapy was administered, and the reasons for non-administration. The data of the 30 patients included in this analysis were used in a previously published study (18).

sec.p: A commercially available immunohistochemistry kit for examining PD-L1 (22C3 pharmDx assay; Dako, Carpinteria, United States) was used to assess the PD-L1 expression in formalin-fixed tumor specimens (19). Biopsy specimens obtained during the cancer diagnosis or before Pemb-Plt-PEM administration were retrieved from the archives. The PD-L1 expression could not be evaluated in some patients.

Patients with a history of ICI treatment including Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy were excluded from the population analysis. The basic therapeutic regimen for all patients was pembrolizumab, the investigator's choice of cisplatin or carboplatin, and pemetrexed for up to six cycles, all administered intravenously, followed by pemetrexed and pembrolizumab in accordance with product labeling. All patients received premedication with folic acid, vitamin B12, and glucocorticoids following the treatment protocols of each institution. In some patients, pembrolizumab or pemetrexed was omitted from pembrolizumab and pemetrexed maintenance therapy based on the physician's decision. First-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy was continued until disease progression, infeasible toxicity, or the withdrawal of consent. Following disease progression during first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy, patients were allowed to choose subsequent treatments.

sec.title: Treatment efficacy
sec.p: The best overall response and maximum tumor shrinkage were recorded as the tumor responses. Radiographic tumor responses were defined according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, version 1.1 (20). The treatment response was evaluated by the attending physician, and no central review was performed.

The NLR was defined as the ratio of the absolute neutrophil to absolute lymphocyte count, and its cutoff was set as 5.0. Patients were classified into 2 groups according to their NLR: low (＜5.0) and high (≥5.0), based on the standards set in most previous reports (14-16).

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: The PFS was measured from the date of Pemb-Plt-PEM initiation until progressive disease (PD) or death. The OS was calculated from day 1 of Pemb-Plt-PEM treatment until death or censoring at the last follow-up. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate the survival, and survival differences were evaluated using the log-rank test. Statistical p values was ＜0.05. Adverse events related to the Pemb-Plt-PEM treatment were evaluated using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 5.0). All statistical analyses were performed using the JMP software program (version 11.0; SAS Institute, Cary, United States).

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: Baseline characteristics of the 30 patients are presented in Table 1. A total of 20 men and 10 women (median age, 76 years old; range, 75-82 years old) were included in the study. The performance status (PS) of the 28 patients (93.3%) was 0-1. Twenty-two (73.3%) patients were current or former smokers. Adenocarcinomas were present in 27 (90.0%) patients. The PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS) was observed in 15 patients (50.0%) with >1% expression. Three patients continued maintenance therapy, either on administration or during follow-up, on the data cutoff date (June 30, 2022).

sec.title: Treatment efficacy and the survival
sec.p: The objective responses to the first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy are shown in Table 2. In brief, 1, 11, 8, and 8 patients showed a complete response, partial response, stable disease, and PD, respectively, during follow-up. The overall response rate (ORR) and disease control rate were 40.0% [95% confidence interval (CI): 24.5-57.7] and 66.7% (95% CI: 48.6-80.8), respectively. The median follow-up time was 14.9 months. The median PFS and OS were 7.5 (95% CI: 2.6-20.7) months and 24.0 (95% CI: 10.7-38.7) months, respectively (Fig. 2a, b). Among the 30 patients, 17 (56.7%) died during follow-up.

The median progression-free survival after the initiation of first-line pembrolizumab plus platinum and pemetrexed was 7.5 (95% confidence interval: 2.6-20.7) months. b) A Kaplan-Meier analysis of the overall survival among the 30 patients. The median overall survival after the start of first-line pembrolizumab plus platinum and pemetrexed was 24.0 (95% confidence interval: 10.7-38.7) months. PFS: progression-free survival

sec.p: We assessed the prognostic value of multiple PFS and OS measurements (Table 3). Univariate analyses demonstrated that the PD-L1 TPS, disease extent at the diagnosis, history of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), and NLR were significantly associated with the PFS. In addition, sex and the NLR were significantly associated with the OS. A multivariate analysis showed that first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy was independently associated with an improved PFS after adjusting for multiple clinical variables and among patients with a low NLR (p=0.01). Notably, the effect of Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy on the median PFS was significantly modified by the NLR (PFS among patients with low and high NLR values: 10.1 and 2.0 months, respectively; log-rank p=0.0056). A multivariate analysis also demonstrated that being a man (p=0.001) and a low NLR (p=0.0003) were independently associated with a favorable OS. Men exhibited a longer median OS than women (32.8 vs. 12.3 months, respectively; log-rank p=0.0051). Similarly, patients with a low NLR had a longer median OS than those with a high NLR (32.8 vs. 2.6 months, respectively; log-rank p=0.0001).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Treatment-related toxicities were evaluated, and the main adverse events during treatment are shown in Table 4. The most common treatment-related adverse event was myelosuppression, with 10%, 6.6%, and 10% of the patients exhibiting grade 3-4 reductions in leukocyte count, neutrophil count, and grade 3-4 anemia, respectively. Febrile neutropenia was not observed. Patients with these conditions either underwent standard supportive therapy or discontinued treatment. The most frequent irAE was a skin rash, but not grade 3-4. Four patients (13.3%) had pneumonitis, three of whom recovered after discontinuing treatment or after taking corticosteroids, whereas one died of potential treatment-related pneumonitis after a cycle of Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy. Grade 3-4 irAEs included adrenal insufficiency and type 1 diabetes mellitus (3.3% each), respectively. Overall, 7 patients (23.3%) discontinued treatment because of adverse events.

sec.title: Relationship between the NLR and treatment efficacy and adverse events
sec.p: We examined efficacy and adverse events while focusing on the NLR, an independent prognostic factor in the multivariate analysis of survival. The ORR for the low- and high-NLR groups were 52.3% (95% CI: 32.3%-71.6%) and 11.1% (95% CI: 0.1%-45.6%), respectively, without any significant difference, although the ORR was higher in the low-NLR group high-NLR group (Supplementary material 1).

Comparisons of the PFS and OS between the low- and high-NLR groups are shown in Supplementary material 2 and 3, respectively. We found a significant association between the NLR and PFS (log-rank p=0.0056; Supplementary material 2) and between the NLR and OS (log-rank p＜0.0001, Supplementary material 3). A comparison of adverse events between the low- and high-NLR groups is presented in Supplementary material 4. The percentages of grade ≥3 adverse events in the low- and high-NLR groups, excluding duplicate events in the same patients, were 42.8% and 44.4%, respectively, without statistical significance (p>0.99). Treatment was discontinued owing to adverse events in 14.2% and 44.4% of the patients in the low- and high-NLR groups, respectively (p=0.15). One treatment-related death occurred in the high-NLR group.

sec.title: Subsequent therapy after PD
sec.p: Five patients did not experience disease progression, two of whom were on a treatment-free follow-up. Three patients received first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy followed by maintenance therapy without PD development at the end of the follow-up period. Table 5 lists the therapies administered following PD, initiated in 25 patients after failure of the first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy. Cytotoxic drug chemotherapy was administered as second-line treatment in 10 patients; 2 patients received docetaxel plus ramucirumab combination therapy, whereas 8 patients received cytotoxic drug (docetaxel, pemetrexed, S-1, or gemcitabine) monotherapy. ICI rechallenge therapy was administered as second-line treatment in three patients: one received ipilimumab and nivolumab combination therapy and two underwent ICI rechallenge monotherapy. The best supportive care instead of second-line chemotherapy was chosen by 12 patients.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study investigated the effectiveness and safety of first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy in elderly patients with non-squamous NSCLC and showed that it was effective and tolerable when maintaining careful patient selection. Specifically, among patients with non-squamous NSCLC ≥75 years old, physicians should consider avoiding Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy in patients with a high NLR.

In a similar patient population, Gandhi et al. reported that the upper limits of the 95% CI crossed 1.00 for patients ≥65 years old (median PFS: 9.0 months vs. 6.7 months; HR: 0.75; 95% CI: 0.55-1.02). Furthermore, a similar risk of PD or death was observed in patients ≥65 years old (HR: 0.64; 95% CI: 0.43-0.95) compared with patients ＜65 years old (HR: 0.43; 95% CI: 0.31-0.61) (7). We found that first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM in elderly patients (≥75 years old) with non-squamous NSCLC was associated with similar ORR (40.0%) and survival time as those in the KEYNOTE-189 study; the ORR in the present study was slightly lower than that in the KEYNOTE-189 study (47.6%), which included non-elderly patients (7). Furthermore, the PFS in this study was 7.5 months, which is slightly shorter than that in a previous prospective study (8.8 months) (7), possibly because of the reflection of real-world clinical practice. Multiple explanations have been suggested for these findings. First, older patients enrolled in this study were frailer and had more comorbidities than the total population with NSCLC. Second, older patients may respond differently from younger patients to immunotherapy because of immunosenescence (21). Senescence is linked to variability in both the congenital and adaptive immune systems (22-24). Although in vitro and in vivo results regarding senescence and immunity are contradictory, several studies have reported that senescence is associated with an overall decrease in T-cell receptors owing to reduced naïve T-cells, along with increased memory T-cell production (24-26). This effect, along with qualitative variability in antigen-presenting cells, predisposes elderly patients to cancer (24). A recent meta-analysis of ICI trials showed no significant age-related differences in the OS, PFS, or adverse events among various cancers (27). The median OS was 24.5 months in this study, which is identical to that reported previously (22.0 months) (9). The ORR, PFS, and OS of single-agent and combination chemotherapy with cytotoxic drugs in Japanese phase III trials for elderly patients with NSCLC (6,28) are shown in Supplementary material 5; first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM in elderly patients with non-squamous NSCLC may ensure a better ORR, PFS, and OS than cytotoxic drugs. Despite the small sample size, Pemb-Plt-PEM showed promising survival outcomes compared with cytotoxic therapy.

The frequency of adverse events causing treatment discontinuation was comparable to that previously reported (7). Although not comparable to the KEYNOTE-189 study, our findings demonstrate that the toxicity of first-line Pemb-Plt-PEMs in elderly patients is similar to that in the aforementioned study (7). While the frequency of grade 5 adverse events in the study remained consistent with previous report (7), the sample size was insufficient to establish a correlation between Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy and treatment-related deaths. These discrepancies underscore the known limitations of clinical trials in evaluating drug safety and the necessity for real-world data (29). Nevertheless, the adverse event profile of Pemb-Plt-PEM in this study was consistent with that reported previously (7) and favorable compared to earlier reports involving cytotoxic drugs among elderly patients (Supplementary material 5) (6,28). The current results indicate that toxicities associated with first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM in elderly patients with non-squamous NSCLC are generally manageable, making it a potential treatment option for the elderly. However, the elderly patients included in this study were selected for Pemb-Plt-PEM in clinical practice based on their good PS and preserved organ function, which is unlikely to apply to all elderly patients with non-squamous NSCLC.

ICIs usually cause fewer adverse events of any grade than conventional cancer therapies (30). However, reports of ICI toxicity in older patients are contradictory. In addition, the efficacy and safety of ICIs alone and in combination with chemotherapy must be evaluated separately. Subset analyses of phase II/III trials involving advanced NSCLC, melanoma, and renal cell carcinoma confirmed that nivolumab was well-tolerated in older patients. However, grade III-V adverse events tended to increase in patients ＞70 years old (31). KEYNOTE analyzed the effectiveness and safety of pembrolizumab in 3,991 patients with melanoma, NSCLC, head and neck cancers, Hodgkin's lymphoma, and urothelial carcinoma. Of these, 46% were ≥65 years old, and 16% were ≥75 years old, with no marked differences in safety between older and younger patients (32). A retrospective study examined the impact of age on the PFS and OS when Pemb-Plt-PEM, pembrolizumab plus carboplatin, and nab-paclitaxel plus paclitaxel were administered (12). No significant difference was observed in the incidence of grade 3-5 non-hematologic and hematologic adverse events between the elderly and non-elderly for both pemetrexed and paclitaxel regimens. However, the incidence of grade 3-5 pneumonitis is significantly higher in the elderly than in younger patients. With the pemetrexed regimen, the elderly showed a higher discontinuation rate owing to adverse events than the non-elderly (48.0% vs. 29.9%, p=0.10), although the difference was not significant (28.0% vs. 12.4%, p=0.07). However, the report included only 25 patients ≥75 years old, and the number of Pemb-Plt-PEM-treated patients was smaller than that in our analysis; thus, the results cannot be definitive. A retrospective study also reported that ICI and chemotherapy combination did not improve survival outcomes in elderly patients with NSCLC and increased the incidence of grade ≥3 irAEs compared with ICIs alone (33). Hence, ICI monotherapy may be recommended for elderly patients with NSCLC and a high PD-L1 expression. However, Pemb-Plt-PEM was not addressed among ICI and chemotherapy combinations in that study, and ICI monotherapy may be considered for patients with high PD-L1 expression. Thus, the appropriate treatment options for patients without high PD-L1 expression remain unclear. Furthermore, which patient subpopulations gain the greatest survival benefit among elderly patients with non-squamous NSCLC treated with first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM also remains unclear.

Atezolizumab plus pemetrexed and platinum-based chemotherapy showed improved efficacy and was well tolerated in Japanese patients ≥75 years old with advanced NSCLC, as shown in the Japanese cohort analysis of the IMpower132 trial (34). Furthermore, a post-hoc analysis showed that the combination therapy of platinum doublet and atezolizumab was tolerable and yielded a favorable PFS and OS among patients ≥75 years old in the integrated population (35). Based on our findings and those of the aforementioned studies, Pemb-Plt-ICI may be a feasible treatment option in patients with non-squamous NSCLC ≥75 years old while ensuring careful patient selection.

The NLR indicates systemic inflammation and immune system balance under malignant biological conditions (36,37). In this study, a high NLR (≥5) was associated with a significantly shorter OS than a low NLR (＜5). In previous real-world studies, patients with chronic inflammation (NLR ≥5) treated with ICIs (monotherapy or combination therapy) showed a poor prognosis (14-16,18). This could be explained by the fact that neutrophils secrete immunosuppressive and angiogenic factors that promote a pro-tumor microenvironment (38). In addition, low numbers of circulating lymphocytes likely result in fewer tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and low antitumor T-cell responses (39). Furthermore, neutrophils participate in inflammatory responses that inhibit antitumor immune responses by suppressing cytotoxic CD8+ T cells (40). Therefore, although the study population was small, Pemb-Plt-PEM may be promising for elderly patients with a low NLR. Furthermore, we observed better OS outcomes in men than in women, with sex as an independent prognostic factor. However, sex did not independently affect the PFS. Immunotherapy benefit patterns among relevant subgroups may vary; for example, a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials across primary tumor sites (41) suggested that ICIs may be less beneficial in women than in men. The modest sample size of our study may have limited our ability to evaluate the relationship between treatment efficacy and gender.

No standardized second-line treatment has been established for elderly patients with non-squamous NSCLC, leaving the impact of second-line or subsequent treatment on the OS unclear. Treatment options for elderly patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC include best supportive care, cytotoxic drugs or ICI monotherapy, and ICI- or platinum-based combination chemotherapy. In this study, 52.0% (13 of 25) of the patients who failed first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy received second-line treatment with anticancer agents. Although elderly patients may receive second-line cytotoxic drug regimens less frequently than their non-elderly counterparts in clinical practice, the use of cytotoxic drug monotherapy rates was relatively high in our cohort (Table 5). In our study, more than half of the patients received a second or subsequent treatment, likely because of age-related impairment of the organ function and potentially complicating comorbid conditions, making Pemb-Plt-PEM a viable first-line option. The reasons for withholding cytotoxic drug therapy in elderly patients include age-related organ function impairment, potentially complicating comorbid conditions, and the likelihood of low tolerance to the toxicity of combination chemotherapy. However, studies on subsequent treatments initiated in elderly patients with non-squamous NSCLC are limited.

Several limitations associated with the present study warrant mention. First, the sample size was small, although a few patients with non-squamous NSCLC ≥75 years old are eligible for Pemb-Plt-PEM in clinical practice. Larger prospective studies are required to verify our results and their applicability in real-world settings. Second, this was a retrospective observational study that analyzed a cohort of older patients. Third, the attending physician could delay or skip the Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy at their discretion. To minimize the effects of these potential sources of bias, all consecutive patients treated at our institutions were included in this study and their medical charts were thoroughly recorded. Fourth, both the use of first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy and selection of subsequent therapy were at the discretion of the treating physician. Selection bias may have been present in the treatment choice, which may have affected the survival after subsequent therapies.

Overall, our results indicate that first-line Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy is effective and feasible in older patients with non-squamous NSCLC. However, our findings suggest that Pemb-Plt-PEM therapy should be avoided in cases of high NLR in patients with non-squamous NSCLC ≥75 years old.

supplementary-material.label: Table S1. Comparison of responses between the low and high NLR groups

caption.p: ORR for the low- and high-NLR groups were 52.3% (95% CI, 32.3–71.6) and 11.1% (95% CI, 0.1–45.6), respectively, without any significant difference, although the ORR was higher in the low-NLR group.

supplementary-material.label: Table S2. Comparison of adverse events between the low and high NLR groups

caption.p: The percentages of grade 3 or higher adverse events in the low- and high-NLR groups, excluding duplicate events in the same patients, were 42.8% and 44.4%, respectively, without statistical significance (p>0.99).

supplementary-material.label: Table S3. Summary of the results of studies on chemotherapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors in elderly patients with non-small cell lung cancer
Figure S1. Kaplan–Meyer curves. Progression-free survival (PFS) of elderly patients treated with pembrolizumab plus platinum and pemetrexed divided into two NLR groups

caption.p: low-NLR (solid line) and high-NLR (dotted line). NLR was significantly associated with PFS (median PFS in patients with low NLR: 10.1 mo; median PFS in patients with high NLR: 2.0 mo; p=0.0056). NLR, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio; HR, hazard ratio; CI, confidence interval.

supplementary-material.label: Figure S2. Kaplan–Meyer curves. The overall survival (OS) of elderly patients treated with pembrolizumab plus platinum and pemetrexed divided into two NLR groups

caption.p: low-NLR (solid line) and high-NLR (dotted line). NLR was significantly associated with OS (median OS in patients with low NLR: 32.8 mo; median OS in patients with high NLR: 2.6 mo; p<0.0001). NLR, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio; HR, hazard ratio; CI, confidence interval.
